specPoints.text: describe the process of micropropagation (tissue culture) in which explants are grown in vitro
understand how micropropagation can be used to produce commercial quantities of genetically identical plants with desirable characteristics

primer.text: Micropropagation turns a tiny shaving of plant tissue into a whole crop of identical plants. This note walks the explant from sterilised cutting to callus to plantlet, then weighs the commercial rewards of the technique against the costs of sterile laboratories and genetic uniformity.

lessons.title: Growing Whole Plants from Tiny Shavings
lessons.opening: Micropropagation turns a tiny shaving of plant tissue into a field of identical plants. Workers cut small explants, sterilise them, and settle them on sterile nutrient agar inside Petri dishes, where the cells multiply into a callus before growth regulators coax whole plantlets into existence.
keyPoints: An explant is a small piece cut from a plant chosen for its useful characteristics.
Explants are sterilised with disinfectant, rinsed in sterile water, and placed on nutrient agar inside a sterile Petri dish.
Explant cells divide on the growth medium into a callus, and fresh medium carrying plant growth regulators steers that callus to grow roots, stems and leaves.
Because the cultures start life in glassware rather than inside a living plant, they are described as grown in vitro.

low.restatement: Cut a shaving, clean it, put it on jelly food, wait for a cell lump, then hormones grow it into a baby plant.
low.analogy: Like starting a whole new bakery from a single scrap of the original sourdough starter, kept clean the whole time.
low.examPointer: Name the stages in order — explant, sterilise, agar, callus, growth regulators, plantlet — examiners award the sequence marks.

medium.restatement: A selected plant yields explants that are surface-sterilised and set on sterile nutrient agar in vitro; their cells proliferate into a callus, and a hormone-rich fresh medium instructs that callus to regenerate roots, stems and leaves as plantlets.
medium.analogy: A nursery that shrinks a whole parent shrub into a fleck of tissue, then persuades that fleck to rebuild itself from scratch on a sterile buffet.
medium.examPointer: Pair every stage with its reason: sterilising defends the culture, agar feeds it, hormones reshape it. Sequence plus justification earns full credit.

check.stem: What name is given to the small pieces of plant tissue cut out to begin a micropropagation culture?

options.text: Explants
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Calluses
options.explanation: A callus is the cell mass that forms later, not the starting piece.

options.text: Plantlets
options.explanation: Plantlets are the rooted young plants produced near the end of the process.

options.text: Plasmids
options.explanation: Plasmids are DNA loops found in bacteria and play no part here.

check.stem: Which outcome follows placing sterilised explants onto sterile nutrient agar in a Petri dish?

options.text: Their cells multiply into a callus
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: They root and flower within days
options.explanation: Roots and shoots come much later, after growth regulators act on the callus.

options.text: They are potted into soil straight away
options.explanation: Potting happens only once plantlets have formed.

options.text: They begin producing seeds
options.explanation: Seed production is never part of tissue culture.

check.stem: What role do plant growth regulators play in the culture?

options.text: They steer the callus so it forms roots, stems and leaves
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: They sterilise the explant surface
options.explanation: A disinfectant rinse does the sterilising before the agar stage.

options.text: They feed the cells as an energy source
options.explanation: Nutrients in the agar feed the cells; regulators direct development.

options.text: They kill bacteria inside the dish
options.explanation: Aseptic technique keeps microbes out; regulators do not kill anything.

check.stem: Why can an explant rebuild a whole plant when a shard of animal tissue cannot?

options.text: Plant cells retain the capacity to differentiate into every specialised type throughout the life of the plant
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Plant cells are simply larger than animal cells
options.explanation: Cell size has nothing to do with regenerating an organism.

options.text: Animal cells contain no DNA
options.explanation: Animal cells do contain DNA; the difference is developmental potential.

options.text: Plant cells divide faster in every situation
options.explanation: Speed of division is not the deciding factor; potential to specialise is.

check.stem: A nursery needs thousands of copies of a disease-resistant orchid during winter. Which micropropagation feature matters most here?

options.text: Clones keep the resistance trait and the laboratory works regardless of season
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Seeds would germinate faster in cold weather
options.explanation: Seed germination is slower and season-bound.

options.text: Each clone would express a different mix of traits
options.explanation: Clones are genetically identical, which is the point.

options.text: Agar releases a pesticide that protects orchids
options.explanation: Agar supplies nutrients; it is not a pesticide.

check.stem: State what the phrase in vitro means when describing tissue culture.
check.modelAnswer: In vitro means the explants are grown outside a living organism, in glassware such as Petri dishes on nutrient agar.

check.stem: Name the cell mass that forms when explant cells divide on the growth medium.
check.modelAnswer: A callus forms as the dividing explant cells build a small mass of cells on the growth medium.

check.stem: Explain why sterilising each explant is a critical early step in micropropagation.
check.modelAnswer: Sterilising removes microbes that would otherwise compete with or infect the culture, so only the wanted plant cells grow across the sterile agar.

check.stem: Fuzzy fungal growth appears on one plate of calluses. Predict the danger to neighbouring plates and justify a response.
check.modelAnswer: Spores could drift onto nearby cultures and ruin them, so the infected calluses should be discarded and aseptic technique reviewed to shield the remaining sterile plates.

lessons.title: Scaling Up: Micropropagation as a Business
lessons.opening: Commercial growers exploit micropropagation to mass-produce identical plants carrying desirable traits, trading the speed, scale and disease-free stock of the laboratory against its running costs and the hazards of a shared genotype.
keyPoints: Plantlets reach maturity sooner than seedlings raised from seed, so new stock reaches the market earlier.
Production runs at any time of year because the laboratory ignores seasons.
Sterile conditions keep the stock disease-free, and a resistance trait held by the parent survives in every clone.
Cloning can bulk up rare species, so the technique also serves conservation programmes.
The costs are real: trained staff, sterile facilities, and a crop in which every plant shares the same weakness to pests and disease.

low.restatement: Same plant, thousands of copies, any month of the year, no diseases — but you need a lab, trained hands, and one bug could wipe out the lot.
low.analogy: A photocopier for plants: perfect copies, endlessly repeatable, yet a single paper jam risk built into every sheet.
low.examPointer: Structure answers as benefit versus drawback pairs — cheap-fast-year-round against lab-cost-uniformity — to hit both marking points.

medium.restatement: Commercially, micropropagation yields large numbers of genetically identical plants quickly, cheaply per square metre and outside any growing season, while preserving parent traits such as disease resistance; the price is skilled labour, sterile infrastructure and zero genetic variation for pests to exploit.
medium.analogy: An industrial kitchen that bakes one perfect cake recipe a thousand times: dependable output, but a single bad ingredient spoils every cake identically.
medium.examPointer: Quote the uniformity drawback with its consequence — vulnerability to the same diseases and pests — because the mark scheme names genetic variation explicitly.

check.stem: Which benefit pair explains why nurseries adopt micropropagation for commercial stock?

options.text: Fast maturity and disease-free plantlets raised in sterile conditions
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Greater genetic diversity and hardier crops
options.explanation: Clones are uniform, so diversity falls rather than rises.

options.text: Lower start-up costs and unskilled labour
options.explanation: The technique demands sterile facilities and trained personnel.

options.text: Harvests tied to natural summer light
options.explanation: The laboratory frees production from seasonal limits.

check.stem: Why must a grower weigh running expenses before committing to micropropagation?

options.text: Sterile laboratories and trained personnel make the technique costly to operate
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Explants must be imported from abroad each season
options.explanation: Explants come from the grower's own chosen plants.

options.text: Agar plates are the dominant expense by far
options.explanation: Costs spread across staff, facilities and materials, not agar alone.

options.text: Insurers charge more for clone-grown crops
options.explanation: Insurance pricing is not part of the taught account.

check.stem: What is the chief biological risk when an entire crop consists of identical clones?

options.text: A single disease or pest able to attack that genotype could devastate every plant at once
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The crop would mutate into new varieties by itself
options.explanation: Clones stay genetically stable; the risk is uniform susceptibility.

options.text: Pollination between the plants becomes impossible
options.explanation: Pollination is not the hazard being described.

options.text: Yields always fall below seed-grown levels
options.explanation: Yields are typically high; the weakness is shared vulnerability.

check.stem: How does micropropagation support plant conservation work?

options.text: Rare species can be multiplied from small tissue samples without depleting wild populations
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: It inserts new genes to strengthen rare species
options.explanation: No new genes are introduced; the parent genome is copied.

options.text: It removes the need for any other conservation method
options.explanation: It complements, rather than replaces, wider conservation efforts.

options.text: It lets rare plants interbreed with common relatives
options.explanation: Cloning produces identical copies, not hybrids.

check.stem: A breeder's best stock carries a leaf virus. Why might micropropagation still deliver clean plants?

options.text: Explants raised in a sterile laboratory yield disease-free plantlets
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Agar chemistry neutralises every virus
options.explanation: The agar feeds the culture; sterile technique excludes contaminants.

options.text: Clones naturally outgrow any viral infection
options.explanation: Growth does not cure infection; exclusion does.

options.text: Freezing the explants destroys viruses
options.explanation: Freezing is not part of the process.

check.stem: State two commercial advantages of producing plants by micropropagation.
check.modelAnswer: It generates large quantities of identical plants cheaply and rapidly, and sterile growing keeps them disease-free.

check.stem: Name the personnel and facility requirements that raise the cost of micropropagation.
check.modelAnswer: Trained personnel and a sterile laboratory are both required, which raises the running cost.

check.stem: Explain why genetic uniformity counts as a disadvantage for a cloned crop.
check.modelAnswer: Uniform clones share one genome, so a disease or pest able to exploit that genotype sweeps through the whole planting with no variation to slow it.

check.stem: A supermarket wants fresh basil in January. Explain how a micropropagation supplier meets that order.
check.modelAnswer: The laboratory operates at any time of year without seasonal limits, so plantlets raised in winter can be grown on under protection to supply January basil.

glossary.definition: A small piece of plant tissue cut from a chosen parent to start a micropropagation culture.
The mass of unspecialised cells that forms when explant cells multiply on growth medium.
Grown outside a living organism, typically in glassware such as Petri dishes.
A young plant with roots, stems and leaves regenerated from a callus.
The technique of growing small pieces of plant tissue on nutrient medium to obtain new plants.
